# helpers4 (Rust) — full reference, version 0.0.10

> Every public item of the `helpers4` crate with its signature, documentation and examples.
> The examples are doctests that run in the crate's CI: treat them as verified usage.
> Import through the module path; names repeat across modules on purpose.
> Each module is a Cargo feature of the same name (`cargo add helpers4 --no-default-features --features <module>`).
> Pre-1.0 (0.x): the split into modules (Cargo features) may change between releases, and the verification tooling is still being extended.

## Module `animation` (Cargo feature `animation`)

Animation timing without a framework: `Easing` curves (the CSS keywords, `cubic-bezier()`,
`steps()` and `linear()`, read from a CSS string or built directly), physical `Spring`s with
their settling time, and `to_css_linear` to turn any curve into a CSS `linear()`.

The same model as the TypeScript package's `animation` category, for code that computes
animation values itself (a renderer, a native player, a tool that exports animations).

### animation::Easing

```rust
pub struct Easing { /* private fields */ }
```

A timing curve: how the progress of an animation follows the progress of time, from `0.0` to
`1.0`. The same curves as CSS `animation-timing-function`.

Build one directly (`linear`, `cubic_bezier`,
`steps`) or read it from a CSS string, e.g. the easing a design tool exported
(`parse`: keywords, `cubic-bezier()`, `steps()` and `linear()`), then evaluate
it with `at`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Easing;

let ease_out = Easing::parse("ease-out")?;
assert!((ease_out.at(0.5) - 0.6846).abs() < 1e-4);

let bouncy = Easing::parse("cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1)")?;
assert!(bouncy.at(0.5) > 1.0); // overshoots before settling
```

#### Easing::cubic_bezier

```rust
pub fn cubic_bezier(x1: f64, y1: f64, x2: f64, y2: f64) -> Option<Self>
```

The curve of CSS `cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`. The `y` values may leave `0..=1` to
overshoot; the `x` values may not, as in CSS.

##### Arguments

- `x1` - x of the first control point, `0.0..=1.0`.
- `y1` - y of the first control point.
- `x2` - x of the second control point, `0.0..=1.0`.
- `y2` - y of the second control point.

##### Returns

The easing, or `None` when an `x` is outside `0.0..=1.0` or a value is not finite.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Easing;

let ease = Easing::cubic_bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1.0);
assert!(ease.is_some_and(|e| (e.at(0.5) - 0.8024).abs() < 1e-4));
assert_eq!(Easing::cubic_bezier(1.5, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0), None);
```

#### Easing::steps

```rust
pub fn steps(count: u32, position: StepPosition) -> Option<Self>
```

The curve of CSS `steps(count, position)`: the progress moves by jumps instead of
continuously, for frame-by-frame sprites, ticking counters or an "instant" transition.

##### Arguments

- `count` - Number of steps, at least `1` (at least `2` with `StepPosition::JumpNone`).
- `position` - Where the jumps happen.

##### Returns

The easing, or `None` for a `count` that is too small.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::{Easing, StepPosition};

let frames = Easing::steps(4, StepPosition::JumpEnd);
assert_eq!(frames.map(|e| e.at(0.6)), Some(0.5));
assert_eq!(Easing::steps(1, StepPosition::JumpNone), None);
```

#### Easing::parse

```rust
pub fn parse(css: &str) -> Result<Self, ParseEasingError>
```

Reads a CSS easing: `linear`, `ease`, `ease-in`, `ease-out`, `ease-in-out`, `step-start`,
`step-end`, `cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, `steps(count[, position])` or
`linear(0, 0.25 40%, 1)` (points with optional input positions, which CSS fills in).

Case and extra spaces are ignored.

##### Arguments

- `css` - The CSS easing.

##### Returns

The easing.

##### Errors

Returns a `ParseEasingError` for anything that is not a CSS easing, or a known function
with arguments CSS rejects.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Easing;

assert_eq!(Easing::parse("linear(0, 0.9 50%, 1)")?.at(0.25), 0.45);
assert_eq!(Easing::parse("steps(4, jump-start)")?.at(0.3), 0.5);
assert!(Easing::parse("bounce").is_err());
```

#### Easing::at

```rust
pub fn at(&self, t: f64) -> f64
```

The progress of the animation at a progress of time.

##### Arguments

- `t` - The progress of time. Clamped to `0.0..=1.0`; a `NaN` counts as `0.0`.

##### Returns

The progress of the animation: `0.0` at the start and `1.0` at the end, possibly outside
`0.0..=1.0` in between for curves that overshoot.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Easing;

let ease = Easing::parse("ease-in-out")?;
assert_eq!(ease.at(0.0), 0.0);
assert!((ease.at(0.5) - 0.5).abs() < 1e-9);
assert_eq!(ease.at(2.0), 1.0);
```

### animation::Spring

```rust
pub struct Spring { /* private fields */ }
```

A damped spring going from `0.0` to `1.0`: the curve behind "spring" transitions of design
tools, with the time it takes to settle.

The motion is solved exactly (under-, critically or over-damped), not by stepping a
simulation, so `at` can be called at any time, in any order.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Spring;

let bouncy = Spring::new(1.0, 300.0, 15.0, 0.0).expect("valid physics");
assert_eq!(bouncy.at(0.0), 0.0);
assert_eq!(bouncy.at(bouncy.duration_ms()), 1.0); // settled
assert!(bouncy.at(bouncy.duration_ms() * 0.3) > 1.0); // overshoots on the way
```

#### Spring::new

```rust
pub fn new(mass: f64, stiffness: f64, damping: f64, initial_velocity: f64) -> Option<Self>
```

A spring from its physical parameters, as design tools (Figma, Framer, …) expose them.

##### Arguments

- `mass` - Mass of the moving object, `> 0`. `1.0` is typical.
- `stiffness` - Stiffness of the spring, `> 0`: higher is faster. `100.0` is typical.
- `damping` - Friction, `> 0`: higher oscillates less. `10.0` is typical.
- `initial_velocity` - Starting speed toward the target, in progress per second.

##### Returns

The spring, or `None` when a parameter is not finite, or `mass`, `stiffness` or `damping`
is not positive, or the spring never settles within a finite time.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Spring;

assert!(Spring::new(1.0, 100.0, 10.0, 0.0).is_some());
assert!(Spring::new(0.0, 100.0, 10.0, 0.0).is_none());
```

#### Spring::duration_ms

```rust
pub fn duration_ms(&self) -> f64
```

The time until the spring settles, from which it stays within `0.001` of its target.

##### Returns

Milliseconds, at least `1.0`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Spring;

let spring = Spring::default();
assert!(spring.duration_ms() > 1000.0 && spring.duration_ms() < 1500.0);
```

#### Spring::at

```rust
pub fn at(&self, time_ms: f64) -> f64
```

The progress at a time: `0.0` at the start, exactly `1.0` from
`duration_ms` on, and possibly above `1.0` while oscillating.

##### Arguments

- `time_ms` - Milliseconds since the start. A time before the start (or `NaN`) gives `0.0`.

##### Returns

The progress.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Spring;

let spring = Spring::default();
assert_eq!(spring.at(-5.0), 0.0);
assert_eq!(spring.at(10_000.0), 1.0);
```

#### Spring::easing

```rust
pub fn easing(&self, t: f64) -> f64
```

The same curve as an easing over `0.0..=1.0`: the fraction of
`duration_ms`, for `to_css_linear` or any
animation that takes an easing function.

##### Arguments

- `t` - The progress of time, `0.0..=1.0`.

##### Returns

The progress.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::Spring;

let spring = Spring::default();
assert_eq!(spring.easing(0.0), 0.0);
assert_eq!(spring.easing(1.0), 1.0);
```

### animation::StepPosition

```rust
pub enum StepPosition {
    /// The first jump happens at the start (CSS `jump-start`, or `start`).
    JumpStart,
    /// The last jump happens at the end, so the first value lasts a whole step (CSS `jump-end`,
    /// or `end`). The default.
    #[default]
    JumpEnd,
    /// No jump at either end: `0` and `1` are each held for a step (CSS `jump-none`).
    JumpNone,
    /// A jump at both ends, so neither `0` nor `1` is held (CSS `jump-both`).
    JumpBoth,
}
```

Where the jumps of a `steps()` easing happen, as in CSS.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::{Easing, StepPosition};

let four_frames = Easing::steps(4, StepPosition::JumpEnd);
assert_eq!(four_frames.map(|e| e.at(0.3)), Some(0.25));
let jump_first = Easing::steps(4, StepPosition::JumpStart);
assert_eq!(jump_first.map(|e| e.at(0.3)), Some(0.5));
```

### animation::to_css_linear

```rust
pub fn to_css_linear(easing: &dyn Fn(f64) -> f64, samples: u32) -> Option<String>
```

Samples an easing function into a CSS `linear()` easing, so that any curve (a
`Spring`, a custom bounce) can be played by CSS transitions and the Web
Animations API, which do not take code.

Values are rounded to 4 decimals. More samples follow the curve more closely, in a longer
string; 32 is smooth for most springs.

#### Arguments

- `easing` - The easing function over `0.0..=1.0`.
- `samples` - Number of points, evenly spaced in time, at least `2`.

#### Returns

A `linear(...)` string, or `None` when `samples` is less than `2`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::{to_css_linear, Spring};

assert_eq!(
    to_css_linear(&|t| t * t, 5).as_deref(),
    Some("linear(0, 0.0625, 0.25, 0.5625, 1)")
);

let spring = Spring::default();
let css = to_css_linear(&|t| spring.easing(t), 32);
assert!(css.is_some_and(|css| css.starts_with("linear(0, ")));
```

### animation::ParseEasingError

```rust
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum ParseEasingError {
    /// Neither an easing keyword nor `cubic-bezier()`, `steps()` or `linear()`.
    UnknownFunction,
    /// A known function with arguments CSS does not accept (a wrong count, a number out of range,
    /// a malformed stop).
    InvalidArguments,
}
```

Why a string is not a CSS easing.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::animation::{Easing, ParseEasingError};

assert_eq!(Easing::parse("bounce"), Err(ParseEasingError::UnknownFunction));
assert_eq!(Easing::parse("steps(0)"), Err(ParseEasingError::InvalidArguments));
```

## Module `ansi` (Cargo feature `ansi`)

ANSI escape sequences: remove them from captured output and build styled text.

`strip`, `contains` and `visible_len` deal with text that already has escape sequences (command
output, logs); `Style` and `Color` build the sequences for colors and attributes. Nothing here
decides whether a terminal supports colors: that stays with the caller.

### ansi::Color

```rust
pub enum Color {
    /// Black.
    Black,
    /// Red.
    Red,
    /// Green.
    Green,
    /// Yellow.
    Yellow,
    /// Blue.
    Blue,
    /// Magenta.
    Magenta,
    /// Cyan.
    Cyan,
    /// White (light grey on most terminals).
    White,
    /// Bright black (dark grey).
    BrightBlack,
    /// Bright red.
    BrightRed,
    /// Bright green.
    BrightGreen,
    /// Bright yellow.
    BrightYellow,
    /// Bright blue.
    BrightBlue,
    /// Bright magenta.
    BrightMagenta,
    /// Bright cyan.
    BrightCyan,
    /// Bright white.
    BrightWhite,
    /// A color of the 256-color palette, `0..=255`.
    Ansi256(u8),
    /// A true color.
    Rgb(u8, u8, u8),
}
```

A terminal color for `Style`.

The 8 standard colors and their bright variants work everywhere; `Color::Ansi256` and
`Color::Rgb` need a terminal that supports 256 or true colors.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ansi::{Color, Style};

assert_eq!(Style::new().fg(Color::Green).paint("ok"), "\u{1b}[32mok\u{1b}[0m");
```

### ansi::contains

```rust
pub fn contains(text: &str) -> bool
```

Whether `text` contains an ANSI escape character (`ESC`, U+001B).

A cheap check for output that is styled, for instance to decide whether to strip it with
`strip` before writing it to a file.

#### Arguments

- `text` - The text to check.

#### Returns

`true` when the text has an escape character.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ansi::contains;

assert!(contains("\u{1b}[32mok\u{1b}[0m"));
assert!(!contains("ok"));
```

### ansi::strip

```rust
pub fn strip(text: &str) -> Cow<'_, str>
```

Removes the ANSI escape sequences from `text`, leaving what a terminal would display.

Handles the colors and styles (`ESC [ ... m`) and every other CSI sequence (cursor moves, erase),
operating system commands such as window titles and hyperlinks (`ESC ] ... BEL` or
`ESC ] ... ESC \`), and the two-character escapes (`ESC c`, `ESC 7`, `ESC ( B`). A lone
escape character is dropped, and a sequence cut short at the end of the text is dropped with
it. Returns the input borrowed, without allocating, when it has no escape character.

#### Arguments

- `text` - The text that may contain escape sequences, such as captured command output.

#### Returns

The text without escape sequences.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ansi::strip;

assert_eq!(strip("\u{1b}[1;31merror\u{1b}[0m: it broke"), "error: it broke");
assert_eq!(strip("plain"), "plain");
```

### ansi::Style

```rust
pub struct Style { /* private fields */ }
```

A text style: colors and attributes, applied to a string with `paint`.

Built by chaining: `Style::new().bold().fg(Color::Red)`. Painting wraps the text in the escape
sequence for the style and a reset (`ESC [ 0 m`); a style with nothing set returns the text
unchanged. This only builds the strings: whether to emit colors at all (a terminal, `NO_COLOR`)
is for the caller to decide.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ansi::{strip, Color, Style};

let error = Style::new().bold().fg(Color::Red);
assert_eq!(error.paint("failed"), "\u{1b}[1;31mfailed\u{1b}[0m");
assert_eq!(strip(&error.paint("failed")), "failed");
```

#### Style::new

```rust
pub fn new() -> Self
```

An empty style: painting with it changes nothing.

##### Returns

A style with no color and no attribute.

#### Style::fg

```rust
pub fn fg(mut self, color: Color) -> Self
```

Sets the text color.

##### Arguments

- `color` - The foreground color.

##### Returns

The style with that text color.

#### Style::bg

```rust
pub fn bg(mut self, color: Color) -> Self
```

Sets the background color.

##### Arguments

- `color` - The background color.

##### Returns

The style with that background.

#### Style::bold

```rust
pub fn bold(mut self) -> Self
```

Makes the text bold.

##### Returns

The style with bold on.

#### Style::dim

```rust
pub fn dim(mut self) -> Self
```

Makes the text dim (faint).

##### Returns

The style with dim on.

#### Style::italic

```rust
pub fn italic(mut self) -> Self
```

Makes the text italic.

##### Returns

The style with italic on.

#### Style::underline

```rust
pub fn underline(mut self) -> Self
```

Underlines the text.

##### Returns

The style with underline on.

#### Style::strikethrough

```rust
pub fn strikethrough(mut self) -> Self
```

Strikes the text through.

##### Returns

The style with strikethrough on.

#### Style::is_plain

```rust
pub fn is_plain(&self) -> bool
```

Whether the style does nothing.

##### Returns

`true` for a style with no color and no attribute.

#### Style::paint

```rust
pub fn paint(&self, text: &str) -> String
```

Applies the style to `text`.

##### Arguments

- `text` - The text to style.

##### Returns

The text between the style's escape sequence and a reset, or the text unchanged for a plain
style.

### ansi::visible_len

```rust
pub fn visible_len(text: &str) -> usize
```

The number of characters a terminal shows for `text`: its length once escape sequences are
removed.

Use it to pad or truncate styled text to a column width. It counts `char`s, not display cells,
so wide characters (CJK, some emoji) count as one and combining marks count too; use a
width-aware crate when you need exact terminal columns.

#### Arguments

- `text` - The text, possibly containing escape sequences.

#### Returns

The number of visible characters.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ansi::visible_len;

assert_eq!(visible_len("\u{1b}[1;31merror\u{1b}[0m"), 5);
assert_eq!(visible_len("plain"), 5);
```

## Module `array` (Cargo feature `array`)

Helpers for slices and `Vec`s that the standard library does not provide.

Inputs are borrowed slices and results are new `Vec`s: nothing is mutated. Membership-based
helpers require `Eq + Hash`. Shuffling and sampling live in the `random` module, where the
generator is an argument.

### array::cartesian_product

```rust
pub fn cartesian_product<A: Clone, B: Clone>(a: &[A], b: &[B]) -> Vec<(A, B)>
```

Returns every pair `(x, y)` with `x` from `a` and `y` from `b`, in row-major order.

For more than two inputs, nest the calls.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The first slice.
- `b` - The second slice.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::cartesian_product;

assert_eq!(
    cartesian_product(&[1, 2], &['a', 'b']),
    vec![(1, 'a'), (1, 'b'), (2, 'a'), (2, 'b')]
);
```

### array::count_by

```rust
pub fn count_by<T, K: Eq + Hash>(items: &[T], mut key: impl FnMut(&T) -> K) -> HashMap<K, usize>
```

Counts the elements of `items` per key returned by `key`.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The elements to count.
- `key` - Returns the key to count each element under.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::count_by;

let counts = count_by(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], |n| if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" });
assert_eq!(counts["odd"], 3);
assert_eq!(counts["even"], 2);
```

### array::difference

```rust
pub fn difference<T: Clone + Eq + Hash>(a: &[T], b: &[T]) -> Vec<T>
```

Returns the elements of `a` that are not in `b`, in `a`'s order.

Duplicates in `a` are kept: only membership in `b` decides whether an element stays.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The elements to keep from.
- `b` - The elements to remove.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::difference;

assert_eq!(difference(&[1, 2, 3, 2], &[2]), vec![1, 3]);
assert_eq!(difference(&[1, 1, 2], &[3]), vec![1, 1, 2]);
```

### array::duplicates

```rust
pub fn duplicates<T: Clone + Eq + Hash>(items: &[T]) -> Vec<T>
```

Returns the elements that appear more than once in `items`, each one once, in the order they
first appear.

The counterpart of `unique`: what `unique` keeps, this reports as repeated.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The elements to scan.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::duplicates;

assert_eq!(duplicates(&[1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2]), vec![1, 2]);
assert_eq!(duplicates(&["a", "b", "c"]), Vec::<&str>::new());
```

### array::equals_unordered

```rust
pub fn equals_unordered<T: Eq + Hash>(a: &[T], b: &[T]) -> bool
```

Returns `true` when `a` and `b` hold the same elements the same number of times, in any order.

Use it for collections where order is meaningless (tags, ids). For positional equality,
compare the slices with `==`.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The first slice.
- `b` - The second slice.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::equals_unordered;

assert!(equals_unordered(&[1, 2, 2, 3], &[3, 2, 1, 2]));
assert!(!equals_unordered(&[1, 2, 2], &[1, 1, 2]));
```

### array::group_by

```rust
pub fn group_by<T: Clone, K: Eq + Hash>(
    items: &[T],
    mut key: impl FnMut(&T) -> K,
) -> HashMap<K, Vec<T>>
```

Groups the elements of `items` by the key returned by `key`.

Within each group, elements keep their original order. The order of the groups themselves is
unspecified (`HashMap`).

#### Arguments

- `items` - The elements to group.
- `key` - Returns the key to group each element under.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::group_by;

let groups = group_by(&[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], |n| n % 2 == 0);
assert_eq!(groups[&true], vec![2, 4]);
assert_eq!(groups[&false], vec![1, 3, 5]);
```

### array::interleave

```rust
pub fn interleave<T: Clone>(a: &[T], b: &[T]) -> Vec<T>
```

Alternates the elements of `a` and `b`, starting with `a`; the leftover of the longer slice
goes at the end.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The slice to take the first, third, … elements from.
- `b` - The slice to take the second, fourth, … elements from.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::interleave;

assert_eq!(interleave(&[1, 3, 5], &[2, 4, 6]), vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]);
assert_eq!(interleave(&["a", "b", "c"], &["x"]), vec!["a", "x", "b", "c"]);
```

### array::intersection

```rust
pub fn intersection<T: Clone + Eq + Hash>(a: &[T], b: &[T]) -> Vec<T>
```

Returns the elements of `a` that also appear in `b`, in `a`'s order.

Duplicates in `a` are kept: only membership in `b` decides whether an element stays.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The first slice.
- `b` - The second slice.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::intersection;

assert_eq!(intersection(&[1, 2, 3, 2], &[2, 3, 4]), vec![2, 3, 2]);
assert_eq!(intersection(&[1], &[2]), Vec::<i32>::new());
```

### array::intersects

```rust
pub fn intersects<T: Eq + Hash>(a: &[T], b: &[T]) -> bool
```

Returns `true` when `a` and `b` share at least one element.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The first slice.
- `b` - The second slice.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::intersects;

assert!(intersects(&[1, 2, 3], &[3, 4]));
assert!(!intersects(&[1, 2], &[3, 4]));
```

### array::key_by

```rust
pub fn key_by<T: Clone, K: Eq + Hash>(items: &[T], mut key: impl FnMut(&T) -> K) -> HashMap<K, T>
```

Indexes the elements of `items` by the key returned by `key`.

When several elements share a key, the last one wins. Use `group_by` to keep
them all.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The elements to index.
- `key` - Returns the key to index each element under.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::key_by;

let users = [("ann", 1), ("bob", 2), ("cat", 1)];
let by_id = key_by(&users, |&(_, id)| id);
assert_eq!(by_id[&2], ("bob", 2));
assert_eq!(by_id[&1], ("cat", 1));
```

### array::replace_or_append

```rust
pub fn replace_or_append<T: Clone>(
    items: &[T],
    item: T,
    matches: impl FnMut(&T) -> bool,
) -> Vec<T>
```

Replaces the first element that matches with `item`, or appends `item` when none does: the
"upsert into a list" gesture.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The current elements.
- `item` - The replacement, or the new element.
- `matches` - Tells which existing element `item` replaces.

#### Returns

A new `Vec`; `items` is not changed.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::replace_or_append;

let users = [(1, "ana"), (2, "bo")];
assert_eq!(
    replace_or_append(&users, (1, "Ana"), |u| u.0 == 1),
    vec![(1, "Ana"), (2, "bo")]
);
assert_eq!(
    replace_or_append(&users, (3, "cy"), |u| u.0 == 3),
    vec![(1, "ana"), (2, "bo"), (3, "cy")]
);
```

### array::symmetric_difference

```rust
pub fn symmetric_difference<T: Clone + Eq + Hash>(a: &[T], b: &[T]) -> Vec<T>
```

Returns the elements present in exactly one of `a` and `b`.

The result is the elements of `a` missing from `b` (in `a`'s order), followed by the elements
of `b` missing from `a` (in `b`'s order). Duplicates are kept.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The first slice.
- `b` - The second slice.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::symmetric_difference;

assert_eq!(symmetric_difference(&[1, 2, 3], &[2, 3, 4]), vec![1, 4]);
```

### array::toggle

```rust
pub fn toggle<T: Clone + PartialEq>(items: &[T], item: T) -> Vec<T>
```

Removes `item` from `items` if it is there, adds it at the end if it is not: the usual
"toggle a selection" gesture. Only the first occurrence is removed.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The current elements.
- `item` - The element to toggle, compared with `==`.

#### Returns

A new `Vec`; `items` is not changed.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::toggle;

assert_eq!(toggle(&[1, 2, 3], 2), vec![1, 3]);
assert_eq!(toggle(&[1, 3], 2), vec![1, 3, 2]);
```

### array::toggle_by

```rust
pub fn toggle_by<T: Clone, K: PartialEq>(
    items: &[T],
    item: T,
    mut key: impl FnMut(&T) -> K,
) -> Vec<T>
```

Like `toggle`, but elements are the same when `key` gives the same value:
toggle objects by id instead of by whole-value equality. Only the first match is removed.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The current elements.
- `item` - The element to add, or whose key to remove.
- `key` - Returns the identity to compare.

#### Returns

A new `Vec`; `items` is not changed.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::toggle_by;

let layers = [("a", 1), ("b", 2)];
// Same id: removed, whatever the other fields hold.
assert_eq!(toggle_by(&layers, ("x", 1), |layer| layer.1), vec![("b", 2)]);
assert_eq!(toggle_by(&layers, ("c", 3), |layer| layer.1), vec![("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3)]);
```

### array::unique

```rust
pub fn unique<T: Clone + Eq + Hash>(items: &[T]) -> Vec<T>
```

Removes duplicate values, keeping the first occurrence of each and the original order.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The elements to deduplicate.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::unique;

assert_eq!(unique(&[1, 2, 1, 3, 2]), vec![1, 2, 3]);
assert_eq!(unique::<i32>(&[]), Vec::<i32>::new());
```

### array::unique_by

```rust
pub fn unique_by<T: Clone, K: Eq + Hash>(items: &[T], mut key: impl FnMut(&T) -> K) -> Vec<T>
```

Removes elements whose `key` was already seen, keeping the first of each key in order.

#### Arguments

- `items` - The elements to deduplicate.
- `key` - Returns the key that decides which elements are duplicates.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::array::unique_by;

let words = ["apple", "avocado", "banana", "blueberry", "cherry"];
assert_eq!(
    unique_by(&words, |w| w.chars().next()),
    vec!["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
);
```

## Module `bytes` (Cargo feature `bytes`)

Helpers for byte slices and sizes that the standard library does not provide.

Reading integers at an offset without panicking, a `ByteReader` cursor for binary formats
(fixed-size values, LEB128 varints, zigzag, NUL-terminated strings), a byte-slice search, a
constant-time comparison, XOR, human-readable sizes (`1.5 KiB`) in both directions, and the
media type of an image from its first bytes or of a file from its extension.

### bytes::ByteReader

```rust
pub struct ByteReader<'a> { /* private fields */ }
```

A cursor over a byte slice, for decoding binary formats: fixed-size integers and floats,
LEB128 varints (signed ones zigzag-encoded), byte runs and NUL-terminated strings.

Every `read_*` method returns `None` when the data is truncated or invalid, and then leaves
the position where it was, so `position` is the offset of the read that
failed: enough to build a precise error in the caller's own error type.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

let data = [0x2a, 0xac, 0x02, b'h', b'i', 0, 0x01, 0x00];
let mut reader = ByteReader::new(&data);
assert_eq!(reader.read_u8(), Some(42));
assert_eq!(reader.read_var_u32(), Some(300));
assert_eq!(reader.read_cstr(), Some("hi"));
assert_eq!(reader.read_u16(Endian::Little), Some(1));
assert_eq!(reader.read_u8(), None); // end of data
assert_eq!(reader.position(), 8);
```

#### ByteReader::read_u8

```rust
pub fn read_u8(&mut self) -> Option<u8>
```

Reads one byte.

##### Returns

The byte, or `None` at the end of the data.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::ByteReader;

let mut reader = ByteReader::new(&[7]);
assert_eq!(reader.read_u8(), Some(7));
assert_eq!(reader.read_u8(), None);
```

#### ByteReader::read_bytes

```rust
pub fn read_bytes(&mut self, len: usize) -> Option<&'a [u8]>
```

Reads `len` bytes, borrowed from the data (no copy).

##### Arguments

- `len` - The number of bytes.

##### Returns

The bytes, or `None` when fewer than `len` remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::ByteReader;

let mut reader = ByteReader::new(b"abc");
assert_eq!(reader.read_bytes(2), Some(&b"ab"[..]));
assert_eq!(reader.read_bytes(2), None);
```

#### ByteReader::read_u16

```rust
pub fn read_u16(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<u16>
```

Reads a `u16` in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 2 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0x12, 0x34]).read_u16(Endian::Big), Some(0x1234));
```

#### ByteReader::read_u32

```rust
pub fn read_u32(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<u32>
```

Reads a `u32` in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 4 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[1, 0, 0, 0]).read_u32(Endian::Little), Some(1));
```

#### ByteReader::read_u64

```rust
pub fn read_u64(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<u64>
```

Reads a `u64` in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 8 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 9]).read_u64(Endian::Big), Some(9));
```

#### ByteReader::read_i16

```rust
pub fn read_i16(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<i16>
```

Reads an `i16` (two's complement) in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 2 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0xff, 0xfe]).read_i16(Endian::Big), Some(-2));
```

#### ByteReader::read_i32

```rust
pub fn read_i32(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<i32>
```

Reads an `i32` (two's complement) in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 4 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0xff; 4]).read_i32(Endian::Little), Some(-1));
```

#### ByteReader::read_i64

```rust
pub fn read_i64(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<i64>
```

Reads an `i64` (two's complement) in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 8 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0xff; 8]).read_i64(Endian::Big), Some(-1));
```

#### ByteReader::read_f32

```rust
pub fn read_f32(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<f32>
```

Reads an IEEE 754 `f32` in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 4 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

let bytes = 1.5f32.to_le_bytes();
assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&bytes).read_f32(Endian::Little), Some(1.5));
```

#### ByteReader::read_f64

```rust
pub fn read_f64(&mut self, endian: Endian) -> Option<f64>
```

Reads an IEEE 754 `f64` in the given byte order.

##### Arguments

- `endian` - The byte order of the value.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 8 bytes remain.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{ByteReader, Endian};

let bytes = (-0.25f64).to_be_bytes();
assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&bytes).read_f64(Endian::Big), Some(-0.25));
```

#### ByteReader::read_var_u32

```rust
pub fn read_var_u32(&mut self) -> Option<u32>
```

Reads an unsigned LEB128 varint of at most 32 bits: 7 bits per byte, least significant
first, the high bit set on every byte but the last.

Overlong encodings (`0x80 0x00` for `0`) are accepted, as most decoders do.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when the data ends inside the varint or the value needs more than
32 bits (a 5th byte above `0x0f`, or a 6th byte).

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::ByteReader;

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0xac, 0x02]).read_var_u32(), Some(300));
assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x0f]).read_var_u32(), Some(u32::MAX));
assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x1f]).read_var_u32(), None);
```

#### ByteReader::read_var_u64

```rust
pub fn read_var_u64(&mut self) -> Option<u64>
```

Reads an unsigned LEB128 varint of at most 64 bits (up to 10 bytes), like
`read_var_u32`.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` when the data ends inside the varint or the value needs more than
64 bits (a 10th byte above `0x01`, or an 11th byte).

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::ByteReader;

let max = [0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x01];
assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&max).read_var_u64(), Some(u64::MAX));
```

#### ByteReader::read_var_i32

```rust
pub fn read_var_i32(&mut self) -> Option<i32>
```

Reads a signed varint: a zigzag-encoded (see `zigzag_decode`) LEB128 varint of at
most 32 bits.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` as for `read_var_u32`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::ByteReader;

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0x01]).read_var_i32(), Some(-1));
assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0x02]).read_var_i32(), Some(1));
```

#### ByteReader::read_var_i64

```rust
pub fn read_var_i64(&mut self) -> Option<i64>
```

Reads a signed varint: a zigzag-encoded (see `zigzag_decode`) LEB128 varint of at
most 64 bits.

##### Returns

The value, or `None` as for `read_var_u64`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::ByteReader;

assert_eq!(ByteReader::new(&[0x03]).read_var_i64(), Some(-2));
```

#### ByteReader::read_cstr

```rust
pub fn read_cstr(&mut self) -> Option<&'a str>
```

Reads a NUL-terminated UTF-8 string and skips the terminating `0`.

##### Returns

The string without its terminator, borrowed from the data, or `None` when there is no
`0` byte before the end or the bytes are not valid UTF-8.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::ByteReader;

let mut reader = ByteReader::new(b"Frame 1\0\0");
assert_eq!(reader.read_cstr(), Some("Frame 1"));
assert_eq!(reader.read_cstr(), Some(""));
assert_eq!(reader.read_cstr(), None);
```

### bytes::constant_time_eq

```rust
pub fn constant_time_eq(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> bool
```

Compares two byte slices without stopping at the first difference.

The loop visits every byte and combines the differences with `|`, so the time it takes does
not depend on where the slices differ, only on their length (a length mismatch returns at
once, so the length is not secret). This is a best effort: Rust and LLVM give no hard
guarantee that a compiler will not turn it back into an early exit, so for cryptographic
code that needs one, use a dedicated crate such as `subtle`.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The first slice.
- `b` - The second slice.

#### Returns

`true` when both slices have the same length and the same content.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::constant_time_eq;

assert!(constant_time_eq(b"secret", b"secret"));
assert!(!constant_time_eq(b"secret", b"secreT"));
assert!(!constant_time_eq(b"secret", b"secre"));
```

### bytes::Endian

```rust
pub enum Endian {
    /// Most significant byte first (network order).
    Big,
    /// Least significant byte first.
    Little,
}
```

The byte order of a multi-byte integer.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{read_u16, Endian};

let bytes = [0x12, 0x34];
assert_eq!(read_u16(&bytes, 0, Endian::Big), Some(0x1234));
assert_eq!(read_u16(&bytes, 0, Endian::Little), Some(0x3412));
```

### bytes::find

```rust
pub fn find(haystack: &[u8], needle: &[u8]) -> Option<usize>
```

The index of the first occurrence of `needle` in `haystack`.

The byte-slice counterpart of `str::find`: the standard library has no subslice search.

#### Arguments

- `haystack` - The bytes to search in.
- `needle` - The bytes to look for.

#### Returns

The starting index of the first match, `Some(0)` for an empty `needle`, or `None` when there
is no match.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::find;

assert_eq!(find(b"hello world", b"o w"), Some(4));
assert_eq!(find(b"hello", b"xyz"), None);
assert_eq!(find(b"hello", b""), Some(0));
```

### bytes::format_size

```rust
pub fn format_size(bytes: u64) -> String
```

Formats a number of bytes with a binary unit and at most one decimal, such as `"1.5 KiB"`.

Units are powers of 1024 (`KiB`, `MiB`, ... `EiB`) and the value is rounded to the nearest
tenth, so `1023.96 KiB` reads `1 MiB` rather than `1024 KiB`. A `.0` is dropped. Only integer
arithmetic is used, so the result never depends on floating-point rounding.
`parse_size` reads it back.

#### Arguments

- `bytes` - The size to format.

#### Returns

The formatted size.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::format_size;

assert_eq!(format_size(512), "512 B");
assert_eq!(format_size(1536), "1.5 KiB");
assert_eq!(format_size(5 * 1024 * 1024), "5 MiB");
assert_eq!(format_size(1_048_575), "1 MiB");
```

### bytes::media_type_of

```rust
pub fn media_type_of(bytes: &[u8]) -> Option<&'static str>
```

Finds the media type of an image from its first bytes (its magic number), whatever its name
says: PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF and SVG. SVG has no magic number, so it is recognized as
text whose first element is `<svg`, possibly after a byte order mark, whitespace, an XML
declaration, comments or a doctype.

#### Arguments

- `bytes` - The start of the file: 512 bytes are enough for every type but a long SVG prolog.

#### Returns

The media type (`"image/png"`, ...), or `None` when it is none of these.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::media_type_of;

assert_eq!(media_type_of(&[0x89, b'P', b'N', b'G', 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a]), Some("image/png"));
assert_eq!(media_type_of(b"<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'/>"), Some("image/svg+xml"));
assert_eq!(media_type_of(b"hello"), None);
```

### bytes::media_type_of_path

```rust
pub fn media_type_of_path(path: &str) -> Option<&'static str>
```

Finds the media type of a file from the extension of its path or URL: images, fonts, web
documents, scripts and styles, data, audio and video. Case is ignored, and a query string or
fragment after the path is skipped. Pass it where a server or a blob needs a `Content-Type`.

#### Arguments

- `path` - A file path or URL.

#### Returns

The media type (`"image/webp"`, ...), or `None` for an unknown or missing extension.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::media_type_of_path;

assert_eq!(media_type_of_path("layers/a@2x.webp"), Some("image/webp"));
assert_eq!(media_type_of_path("/fonts/Inter.WOFF2?v=3"), Some("font/woff2"));
assert_eq!(media_type_of_path("LICENSE"), None);
```

### bytes::parse_size

```rust
pub fn parse_size(input: &str) -> Result<u64, ParseSizeError>
```

Parses a human-written size such as `"1.5 KiB"`, `"10MB"` or `"512"` into a number of bytes.

The number is a non-negative decimal (a fraction is allowed, at most 18 decimal digits are
used, and the result is rounded down), optionally followed by whitespace and a unit, matched
without regard to case:

- none or `B`: bytes;
- `KiB`, `MiB`, `GiB`, `TiB`, `PiB`, `EiB`, and the single letters `K`, `M`, `G`, `T`, `P`,
  `E`: powers of 1024;
- `KB`, `MB`, `GB`, `TB`, `PB`, `EB`: powers of 1000.

`format_size` writes the binary form back.

#### Arguments

- `input` - The size to parse.

#### Errors

Returns a `ParseSizeError` for an empty string, something other than a number where one is
expected, an unknown unit, or a size that does not fit in a `u64`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::parse_size;

assert_eq!(parse_size("1.5 KiB"), Ok(1536));
assert_eq!(parse_size("10MB"), Ok(10_000_000));
assert_eq!(parse_size("512"), Ok(512));
assert!(parse_size("ten").is_err());
```

### bytes::read_u16

```rust
pub fn read_u16(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize, endian: Endian) -> Option<u16>
```

Reads a `u16` from `bytes` at `offset`, in the given byte order.

#### Arguments

- `bytes` - The buffer to read from.
- `offset` - The index of the first byte to read.
- `endian` - The byte order of the value in the buffer.

#### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 2 bytes remain at `offset`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{read_u16, Endian};

let bytes = [0x12, 0x34];
assert_eq!(read_u16(&bytes, 0, Endian::Big), Some(0x1234));
assert_eq!(read_u16(&bytes, 0, Endian::Little), Some(0x3412));
assert_eq!(read_u16(&bytes, 1, Endian::Big), None);
```

### bytes::read_u32

```rust
pub fn read_u32(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize, endian: Endian) -> Option<u32>
```

Reads a `u32` from `bytes` at `offset`, in the given byte order.

#### Arguments

- `bytes` - The buffer to read from.
- `offset` - The index of the first byte to read.
- `endian` - The byte order of the value in the buffer.

#### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 4 bytes remain at `offset`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{read_u32, Endian};

let bytes = [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78];
assert_eq!(read_u32(&bytes, 0, Endian::Big), Some(0x1234_5678));
assert_eq!(read_u32(&bytes, 0, Endian::Little), Some(0x7856_3412));
assert_eq!(read_u32(&bytes, 1, Endian::Big), None);
```

### bytes::read_u64

```rust
pub fn read_u64(bytes: &[u8], offset: usize, endian: Endian) -> Option<u64>
```

Reads a `u64` from `bytes` at `offset`, in the given byte order.

#### Arguments

- `bytes` - The buffer to read from.
- `offset` - The index of the first byte to read.
- `endian` - The byte order of the value in the buffer.

#### Returns

The value, or `None` when fewer than 8 bytes remain at `offset`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::{read_u64, Endian};

let bytes = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0];
assert_eq!(read_u64(&bytes, 0, Endian::Big), Some(256));
assert_eq!(read_u64(&bytes, 0, Endian::Little), Some(0x0001_0000_0000_0000));
assert_eq!(read_u64(&bytes, 1, Endian::Big), None);
```

### bytes::xor

```rust
pub fn xor(a: &[u8], b: &[u8]) -> Option<Vec<u8>>
```

The bytewise XOR of two slices of the same length.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The first slice.
- `b` - The second slice.

#### Returns

A new `Vec` whose byte `i` is `a[i] ^ b[i]`, or `None` when the lengths differ.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::xor;

assert_eq!(xor(&[0b1100, 0b1010], &[0b1010, 0b1010]), Some(vec![0b0110, 0]));
assert_eq!(xor(&[1], &[1, 2]), None);
```

### bytes::zigzag_decode

```rust
pub fn zigzag_decode(value: u64) -> i64
```

Reverses `zigzag_encode`: `0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...` become
`0, -1, 1, -2, 2, ...`.

#### Arguments

- `value` - The zigzag-encoded value.

#### Returns

The signed integer. A value read from a 32-bit varint always fits in an `i32`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::zigzag_decode;

assert_eq!(zigzag_decode(0), 0);
assert_eq!(zigzag_decode(1), -1);
assert_eq!(zigzag_decode(2), 1);
assert_eq!(zigzag_decode(u64::MAX), i64::MIN);
```

### bytes::zigzag_encode

```rust
pub fn zigzag_encode(value: i64) -> u64
```

Maps a signed integer to an unsigned one so that small magnitudes stay small: `0, -1, 1, -2,
2, ...` become `0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...`. Varint formats (Protocol Buffers `sint`, Kiwi) encode
signed values this way before LEB128, so that `-1` takes one byte instead of ten.

The result does not depend on the integer width: an `i32` widened to `i64` encodes to the
same value as with 32-bit zigzag.

#### Arguments

- `value` - The signed integer.

#### Returns

The zigzag-encoded value; `zigzag_decode` reverses it.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::bytes::zigzag_encode;

assert_eq!(zigzag_encode(0), 0);
assert_eq!(zigzag_encode(-1), 1);
assert_eq!(zigzag_encode(1), 2);
assert_eq!(zigzag_encode(i64::MIN), u64::MAX);
```

### bytes::ParseSizeError

```rust
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum ParseSizeError {
    /// The string is empty or only whitespace.
    Empty,
    /// A number was expected but something else was found.
    ExpectedNumber {
        /// Byte offset of the offending character in the input.
        index: usize,
    },
    /// The unit is not one of the known ones (`B`, `KB`, `KiB`, `K`, ...).
    UnknownUnit {
        /// Byte offset of the unit in the input.
        index: usize,
    },
    /// The size does not fit in a `u64`.
    Overflow,
}
```

Why a string could not be parsed as a size.

## Module `cache` (Cargo feature `cache`)

Caches and stores: entries that expire with a passed-in clock (`ExpiringMap`), and a
capacity-bounded map that evicts by recency instead (`LruCache`). Neither ever reads a
clock or the system allocator's notion of "recent" behind the caller's back.

### cache::ExpiringMap

```rust
pub struct ExpiringMap<K, V, T = u64> { /* private fields */ }
```

A map whose entries expire, with the clock passed in by the caller.

Nothing here reads a clock, so it is trivially testable and works with any timestamp: pass
unix seconds (`u64`, e.g. the `exp` of a token), milliseconds, or an `Instant`. An entry is
live while `now < expires_at`. Expired entries are dropped lazily: every write sweeps them, so
the map only grows with the entries inserted inside one lifetime window (a replay-protection
store keyed by token id, a cache of pending challenges, ...).

The sweep is skipped in constant time while nothing can have expired yet, and is a single pass
otherwise. `len` counts entries still stored, expired or not, until the next write sweeps them:
call `evict_expired` first when comparing it to a threshold.

There is **no capacity bound**. If the keys come from untrusted input and their lifetimes are
long, the number of live entries is only limited by the insert rate times the lifetime: bound
it yourself (reject or rate-limit inserts) when that matters.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::cache::ExpiringMap;

let mut seen: ExpiringMap<&str, (), u64> = ExpiringMap::new();
let now = 1_000;

// First use of a token id, valid until t = 1_060: accepted.
assert!(seen.insert_if_absent("jti-1", (), 1_060, now));
// The same id again while it is live: a replay.
assert!(!seen.insert_if_absent("jti-1", (), 1_060, now + 10));
// Once it has expired it can be used (and remembered) again.
assert!(seen.insert_if_absent("jti-1", (), 1_200, 1_060));
```

#### ExpiringMap::new

```rust
pub fn new() -> Self
```

Creates an empty map.

##### Returns

A new, empty `ExpiringMap`.

#### ExpiringMap::len

```rust
pub fn len(&self) -> usize
```

The number of stored entries, including expired ones that no write has swept yet.

##### Returns

The number of entries currently stored, including any that have expired but were not evicted yet.

#### ExpiringMap::is_empty

```rust
pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool
```

Whether nothing is stored (see `len`).

##### Returns

`true` when the map stores no entries at all, including expired ones not yet evicted.

#### ExpiringMap::clear

```rust
pub fn clear(&mut self)
```

Removes every entry, expired or not.

#### ExpiringMap::insert

```rust
pub fn insert(&mut self, key: K, value: V, expires_at: T, now: T) -> Option<V>
```

Stores `value` under `key` until `expires_at`, replacing any live entry, and returns the
replaced value. Expired entries are swept first. An `expires_at` that is not after `now`
expires immediately.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to store the value under.
- `value` - The value to store.
- `expires_at` - The point in time at which the entry becomes invisible.
- `now` - The current time, used to evict already-expired entries before inserting.

##### Returns

The previous value for `key`, if there was one and it had not expired yet.

#### ExpiringMap::insert_if_absent

```rust
pub fn insert_if_absent(&mut self, key: K, value: V, expires_at: T, now: T) -> bool
```

Stores `value` under `key` only if there is no live entry for it, and returns whether it
did. This is the replay check: `false` means the key was already seen and is still live.
Expired entries are swept first.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to store the value under.
- `value` - The value to store.
- `expires_at` - The point in time at which the entry becomes invisible.
- `now` - The current time, used to decide whether an existing entry has already expired.

##### Returns

`true` when the value was inserted, `false` when `key` already had a live entry.

#### ExpiringMap::get

```rust
pub fn get(&self, key: &K, now: T) -> Option<&V>
```

The live value under `key`, or `None` if absent or expired at `now`.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to look up.
- `now` - The current time, used to decide whether the entry has expired.

##### Returns

The value for `key`, or `None` when it is missing or expired.

#### ExpiringMap::contains_key

```rust
pub fn contains_key(&self, key: &K, now: T) -> bool
```

Whether there is a live entry under `key` at `now`.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to look up.
- `now` - The current time, used to decide whether the entry has expired.

##### Returns

`true` when `key` has a live entry.

#### ExpiringMap::remove

```rust
pub fn remove(&mut self, key: &K, now: T) -> Option<V>
```

Removes `key` and returns its value if it was still live at `now`.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to remove.
- `now` - The current time, used to decide whether the entry had already expired.

##### Returns

The removed value, or `None` when there was no live entry for `key`.

#### ExpiringMap::evict_expired

```rust
pub fn evict_expired(&mut self, now: T) -> usize
```

Drops every entry that has expired at `now` and returns how many. Writes do this already;
call it directly to release memory while nothing is being written.

##### Arguments

- `now` - The current time.

##### Returns

The number of entries removed.

### cache::ExpiringSet

```rust
pub type ExpiringSet<K, T = u64> = ExpiringMap<K, (), T>
```

A set whose members expire: an `ExpiringMap` without values.

### cache::LruCache

```rust
pub struct LruCache<K, V> { /* private fields */ }
```

A map bounded to at most `capacity` entries: once full, inserting a new key evicts the least
recently used one.

"Used" means read with `get` or `get_or_insert_with`,
or written with `insert`; `contains_key` does not count,
so checking for a key without reading it never changes what gets evicted next.

Unlike `ExpiringMap`, entries never expire on their own: eviction is
only ever "the entry nobody has touched in the longest time", driven purely by capacity.

A capacity of `0` is a documented degenerate case, not an error: the cache never stores
anything, and every `insert` is immediately evicted.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::cache::LruCache;

let mut cache: LruCache<&str, i32> = LruCache::new(2);
cache.insert("a", 1);
cache.insert("b", 2);
cache.get(&"a"); // touch "a": "b" is now the least recently used
cache.insert("c", 3); // evicts "b", not "a"
assert_eq!(cache.get(&"a"), Some(&1));
assert_eq!(cache.get(&"b"), None);
assert_eq!(cache.get(&"c"), Some(&3));
```

#### LruCache::new

```rust
pub fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self
```

Creates an empty cache holding at most `capacity` entries.

##### Arguments

- `capacity` - The most entries the cache holds before it starts evicting.

##### Returns

An empty cache.

#### LruCache::get

```rust
pub fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<&V>
```

The live value for `key`, marking it as just used.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to look up.

##### Returns

The value for `key`, or `None` when it is not present.

#### LruCache::insert

```rust
pub fn insert(&mut self, key: K, value: V) -> Option<V>
```

Inserts `value` under `key`, marking it as just used.

Evicts the least recently used entry first when `key` is new and the cache is already at
capacity.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to insert or update.
- `value` - The value to store.

##### Returns

The previous value stored under `key`, if any.

#### LruCache::contains_key

```rust
pub fn contains_key(&self, key: &K) -> bool
```

Whether `key` has a live entry, without affecting eviction order.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to check.

##### Returns

`true` when `key` has a live entry.

#### LruCache::len

```rust
pub fn len(&self) -> usize
```

How many entries are currently stored.

##### Returns

The number of live entries, at most `capacity`.

#### LruCache::is_empty

```rust
pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool
```

Whether the cache holds no entries.

##### Returns

`true` when `len` is `0`.

#### LruCache::capacity

```rust
pub fn capacity(&self) -> usize
```

The capacity this cache was created with.

##### Returns

The most entries the cache holds before it starts evicting.

#### LruCache::clear

```rust
pub fn clear(&mut self)
```

Removes every entry.

#### LruCache::get_or_insert_with

```rust
pub fn get_or_insert_with(&mut self, key: K, f: impl FnOnce() -> V) -> V
```

Returns the value for `key`, computing and storing it with `f` first if absent.

Bounded, single-key equivalent of `Memoize`: the same key
never recomputes while it stays in the cache, but an old key can be evicted to make room.
With a capacity of `0` the freshly computed value is still returned, but is not retained
(nothing is, see `new`): the next call recomputes it.

##### Arguments

- `key` - The key to look up.
- `f` - Computes the value to store when `key` is absent. Not called when `key` is
  already present.

##### Returns

The value for `key`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::cache::LruCache;

let mut calls = 0;
let mut cache: LruCache<u32, u32> = LruCache::new(4);
let square = |cache: &mut LruCache<u32, u32>, n: u32, calls: &mut i32| {
    cache.get_or_insert_with(n, || {
        *calls += 1;
        n * n
    })
};
assert_eq!(square(&mut cache, 7, &mut calls), 49);
assert_eq!(square(&mut cache, 7, &mut calls), 49); // served from the cache
assert_eq!(calls, 1);
```

## Module `ci` (Cargo feature `ci`)

Detecting CI environments and reporting pipeline status.

`detect`, `is_ci` and `is_pull_request` take the environment as a lookup function instead of reading it,
so they are as easy to test as to use (`&|name| std::env::var(name).ok()`). `Status`, `overall` and
`render_report` turn job results into the Markdown summary of a PR comment.

### ci::detect

```rust
pub fn detect(get: &dyn Fn(&str) -> Option<String>) -> Option<Provider>
```

Which CI service the environment belongs to, if any.

The environment is a parameter, not read behind your back: pass a lookup such as
`&|name| std::env::var(name).ok()`, or a closure over a map in a test. The known services are
recognized by their own variables (`GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `GITLAB_CI`, `CIRCLECI`, ...); any other
environment with a truthy `CI` variable is `Provider::Other`. A variable is truthy unless it
is empty, `0` or `false` (case-insensitive).

#### Arguments

- `get` - Looks a variable up by name.

#### Returns

The `Provider`, or `None` outside CI.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ci::{detect, Provider};

let env = |name: &str| (name == "GITHUB_ACTIONS").then(|| "true".to_string());
assert_eq!(detect(&env), Some(Provider::GitHubActions));
assert_eq!(detect(&|_: &str| None), None);
```

### ci::is_ci

```rust
pub fn is_ci(get: &dyn Fn(&str) -> Option<String>) -> bool
```

Whether the environment looks like a CI run.

The same as `detect(get).is_some()`. The environment is a parameter: pass
`&|name| std::env::var(name).ok()` for the real one.

#### Arguments

- `get` - Looks a variable up by name.

#### Returns

`true` when a known CI service, or a truthy `CI` variable, is present.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ci::is_ci;

assert!(is_ci(&|name: &str| (name == "CI").then(|| "true".to_string())));
assert!(!is_ci(&|_: &str| None));
```

### ci::is_pull_request

```rust
pub fn is_pull_request(get: &dyn Fn(&str) -> Option<String>) -> bool
```

Whether the current CI run was triggered by a pull request (or merge request).

It looks at the variable each service sets for that: `GITHUB_EVENT_NAME` (`pull_request` or
`pull_request_target`), `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_IID` on GitLab, `CIRCLE_PULL_REQUEST`,
`TRAVIS_PULL_REQUEST`, `BUILDKITE_PULL_REQUEST`, `SYSTEM_PULLREQUEST_PULLREQUESTID` on Azure,
`BITBUCKET_PR_ID`, `DRONE_PULL_REQUEST`, `APPVEYOR_PULL_REQUEST_NUMBER`, `PULL_REQUEST` on
Netlify and `VERCEL_GIT_PULL_REQUEST_ID`. Services without a known variable (Jenkins,
TeamCity, ...) and any environment outside CI give `false`.

#### Arguments

- `get` - Looks a variable up by name.

#### Returns

`true` for a pull request run.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ci::is_pull_request;

let env = |name: &str| match name {
    "GITHUB_ACTIONS" => Some("true".to_string()),
    "GITHUB_EVENT_NAME" => Some("pull_request".to_string()),
    _ => None,
};
assert!(is_pull_request(&env));
```

### ci::overall

```rust
pub fn overall(statuses: &[Status]) -> Status
```

The single status that sums up several: the worst one wins.

A failure beats everything, then a cancellation, then anything still pending; when everything
that ran succeeded the result is success, skipped jobs not counting against it. A list where
every job was skipped, and an empty list, sum up to `Status::Skipped` (nothing ran).

#### Arguments

- `statuses` - The statuses of the jobs.

#### Returns

The overall status.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ci::{overall, Status};

assert_eq!(overall(&[Status::Success, Status::Skipped]), Status::Success);
assert_eq!(overall(&[Status::Success, Status::Failure, Status::Pending]), Status::Failure);
assert_eq!(overall(&[]), Status::Skipped);
```

### ci::Provider

```rust
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum Provider {
    /// GitHub Actions.
    GitHubActions,
    /// GitLab CI/CD.
    GitLabCi,
    /// CircleCI.
    CircleCi,
    /// Travis CI.
    TravisCi,
    /// Buildkite.
    Buildkite,
    /// Azure Pipelines.
    AzurePipelines,
    /// Bitbucket Pipelines.
    BitbucketPipelines,
    /// Drone.
    Drone,
    /// TeamCity.
    TeamCity,
    /// AppVeyor.
    AppVeyor,
    /// AWS CodeBuild.
    AwsCodeBuild,
    /// Jenkins.
    Jenkins,
    /// Netlify builds.
    Netlify,
    /// Vercel builds.
    Vercel,
    /// Cloudflare Pages builds.
    CloudflarePages,
    /// An unrecognized service that sets the conventional `CI` variable.
    Other,
}
```

A continuous-integration service, as recognized by `detect`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ci::Provider;

assert_eq!(Provider::GitHubActions.name(), "GitHub Actions");
```

#### Provider::name

```rust
pub fn name(self) -> &'static str
```

The service name as its vendor writes it.

##### Returns

For instance `"GitHub Actions"`; `"CI"` for `Provider::Other`.

### ci::render_report

```rust
pub fn render_report(title: &str, jobs: &[(&str, Status)]) -> String
```

A Markdown summary of a pipeline, ready for a PR comment or a job summary.

One heading with the overall status (the worst of the jobs, see `overall`),
then a table with one row per job in the order given: its icon, name and status. A `|` in a job
name is escaped and line breaks in the title or a name become spaces, so nothing can break the
table. There is no trailing newline.

#### Arguments

- `title` - The heading, such as `"Pull Request Validation"`.
- `jobs` - The jobs with their status, as `(name, status)`.

#### Returns

The Markdown text.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ci::{render_report, Status};

let report = render_report("Validation", &[("build", Status::Success), ("tests", Status::Failure)]);
assert!(report.starts_with("### \u{274c} Validation"));
assert!(report.contains("| \u{2705} | build | `success` |"));
```

### ci::Status

```rust
pub enum Status {
    /// Finished without errors.
    Success,
    /// Finished with an error, or timed out.
    Failure,
    /// Stopped before it finished.
    Cancelled,
    /// Not run.
    Skipped,
    /// Queued or still running.
    Pending,
}
```

The outcome of a CI job or step.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::ci::Status;

assert_eq!(Status::from_conclusion("failure"), Some(Status::Failure));
assert_eq!(Status::Success.icon(), "\u{2705}");
assert_eq!(Status::Success.label(), "success");
```

#### Status::from_conclusion

```rust
pub fn from_conclusion(conclusion: &str) -> Option<Self>
```

Reads the conclusion names CI services use, ignoring case.

`success`, `passed` and `pass` are `Status::Success`; `failure`, `failed`, `error` and
`timed_out` are `Status::Failure`; `cancelled` and `canceled` are `Status::Cancelled`;
`skipped` is `Status::Skipped`; `pending`, `queued`, `in_progress` and `running` are
`Status::Pending`.

##### Arguments

- `conclusion` - The name, such as `"success"` or `"cancelled"`.

##### Returns

The status, or `None` for a name that is not one of those.

#### Status::icon

```rust
pub fn icon(self) -> &'static str
```

An emoji for the status, for a report or a PR comment.

##### Returns

`\u{2705}` for success, `\u{274c}` for failure, `\u{1f6ab}` for cancelled, `\u{23ed}\u{fe0f}` for skipped
and `\u{23f3}` for pending.

#### Status::label

```rust
pub fn label(self) -> &'static str
```

The lower-case name of the status.

##### Returns

`"success"`, `"failure"`, `"cancelled"`, `"skipped"` or `"pending"`.

## Module `color` (Cargo feature `color`)

Colors without a dependency: parsing, hex, CSS output, HSL, alpha, blending and WCAG contrast.

`Rgb` is an 8-bit sRGB color that parses from `#rgb`, `#rrggbb`, `rgb(r, g, b)` or a basic CSS name;
`Hsl` converts to and from it; `mix` blends two colors; `contrast_ratio` and `best_text_color` answer
"is this text readable on that background".

### color::best_text_color

```rust
pub fn best_text_color(background: Rgb) -> Rgb
```

Picks black or white text, whichever contrasts more with `background`.

Compares the WCAG `contrast_ratio` of both and returns the winner
(black on a tie), so the text stays as readable as it can be without you choosing a color per
background by hand.

#### Arguments

- `background` - The color the text will sit on.

#### Returns

Black (`#000000`) or white (`#ffffff`).

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{best_text_color, Rgb};

assert_eq!(best_text_color(Rgb::parse("#ffeb3b")?), Rgb::new(0, 0, 0)); // on yellow
assert_eq!(best_text_color(Rgb::parse("#0d47a1")?), Rgb::new(255, 255, 255)); // on dark blue
```

### color::BlendMode

```rust
#[non_exhaustive]
pub enum BlendMode {
    /// The source replaces the backdrop (a plain alpha composite). The default.
    #[default]
    Normal,
    /// Multiplies the channels: always darker.
    Multiply,
    /// The inverse of [`Multiply`](Self::Multiply): always lighter.
    Screen,
    /// [`Multiply`](Self::Multiply) or [`Screen`](Self::Screen) depending on the backdrop.
    Overlay,
    /// The darker of the two, per channel.
    Darken,
    /// The lighter of the two, per channel.
    Lighten,
    /// Brightens the backdrop to reflect the source.
    ColorDodge,
    /// Darkens the backdrop to reflect the source.
    ColorBurn,
    /// [`Multiply`](Self::Multiply) or [`Screen`](Self::Screen) depending on the source.
    HardLight,
    /// A softer [`HardLight`](Self::HardLight).
    SoftLight,
    /// The absolute difference of the two.
    Difference,
    /// Like [`Difference`](Self::Difference), with less contrast.
    Exclusion,
    /// The hue of the source with the saturation and luminosity of the backdrop.
    Hue,
    /// The saturation of the source with the hue and luminosity of the backdrop.
    Saturation,
    /// The hue and saturation of the source with the luminosity of the backdrop.
    Color,
    /// The luminosity of the source with the hue and saturation of the backdrop.
    Luminosity,
}
```

The blend modes of the W3C Compositing and Blending specification, the same ones as CSS
`mix-blend-mode`. The last four (`Hue`, `Saturation`,
`Color`, `Luminosity`) are non-separable: they mix the
three channels together instead of one channel at a time.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::BlendMode;

assert_eq!(BlendMode::default(), BlendMode::Normal);
```

### color::blend

```rust
pub fn blend(backdrop: Rgba, source: Rgba, mode: BlendMode) -> Rgba
```

Composites a source color over a backdrop with a blend mode, as the browser does for
`mix-blend-mode` (W3C Compositing and Blending Level 1, source-over). Both colors are straight
(non-premultiplied); the maths run in premultiplied space and the result is straight again,
each channel and the alpha rounded to the nearest 8-bit value.

#### Arguments

- `backdrop` - The color underneath.
- `source` - The color painted over it.
- `mode` - The blend mode; `BlendMode::Normal` is a plain alpha composite.

#### Returns

The straight result. Transparent black when both colors are fully transparent.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{blend, BlendMode, Rgba};

let red = Rgba::new(255, 0, 0, 255);
let half_blue = Rgba::new(0, 0, 255, 128);
assert_eq!(blend(red, half_blue, BlendMode::Normal), Rgba::new(127, 0, 128, 255));

let orange = Rgba::new(200, 100, 50, 255);
let gray = Rgba::new(100, 100, 100, 255);
assert_eq!(blend(orange, gray, BlendMode::Multiply), Rgba::new(78, 39, 20, 255));
```

### color::contrast_ratio

```rust
pub fn contrast_ratio(a: Rgb, b: Rgb) -> f64
```

The WCAG contrast ratio between two colors, from `1.0` (identical) to `21.0` (black on white).

It is `(L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05)` where `L1` is the relative luminance of the lighter color
and `L2` of the darker one, so the order of the arguments does not matter. WCAG 2.x asks for
at least `4.5` for normal text and `3.0` for large text (level AA), `7.0` and `4.5` for AAA.

#### Arguments

- `a` - One color, for instance the text.
- `b` - The other color, for instance its background.

#### Returns

The ratio, `1.0..=21.0`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{contrast_ratio, Rgb};

let ratio = contrast_ratio(Rgb::new(0, 0, 0), Rgb::new(255, 255, 255));
assert!((ratio - 21.0).abs() < 1e-9);
assert!(contrast_ratio(Rgb::parse("#767676")?, Rgb::new(255, 255, 255)) >= 4.5);
```

### color::Hsb

```rust
pub struct Hsb { /* private fields */ }
```

A color as hue, saturation and brightness (also called HSV), the model of design tool color
pickers. Unlike `Hsl` lightness, brightness `1.0` is the pure color, not white.

The hue is in degrees, `0.0..360.0`; saturation and brightness are fractions from `0.0` to
`1.0`. `Hsb::new` brings any input into those ranges. Get one from `Rgb::to_hsb` and go
back with `Hsb::to_rgb`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{Hsb, Rgb};

assert_eq!(Hsb::new(0.0, 1.0, 1.0).to_rgb(), Rgb::new(255, 0, 0));
assert_eq!(Rgb::new(0, 128, 128).to_hsb(), Hsb::new(180.0, 1.0, 128.0 / 255.0));
```

#### Hsb::new

```rust
pub fn new(h: f64, s: f64, b: f64) -> Self
```

Builds a color, normalizing the values: the hue wraps around 360 degrees, saturation and
brightness are clamped to `0.0..=1.0`, and a `NaN` counts as `0.0`.

##### Arguments

- `h` - The hue in degrees.
- `s` - The saturation, `0.0` (grey) to `1.0` (vivid).
- `b` - The brightness, `0.0` (black) to `1.0` (the pure color).

##### Returns

The normalized color.

#### Hsb::h

```rust
pub fn h(self) -> f64
```

The hue in degrees.

##### Returns

A value in `0.0..360.0`.

#### Hsb::s

```rust
pub fn s(self) -> f64
```

The saturation.

##### Returns

A value from `0.0` to `1.0`.

#### Hsb::b

```rust
pub fn b(self) -> f64
```

The brightness.

##### Returns

A value from `0.0` to `1.0`.

#### Hsb::to_rgb

```rust
pub fn to_rgb(self) -> Rgb
```

The nearest 8-bit sRGB color.

##### Returns

The `Rgb` color, each channel rounded to the nearest integer.

### color::Hsl

```rust
pub struct Hsl { /* private fields */ }
```

A color as hue, saturation and lightness.

The hue is in degrees, `0.0..360.0`; saturation and lightness are fractions from `0.0` to `1.0`.
`Hsl::new` brings any input into those ranges. Get one from `Rgb::to_hsl` and go back with
`Hsl::to_rgb`.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{Hsl, Rgb};

let teal = Hsl::new(180.0, 1.0, 0.25);
assert_eq!(teal.to_rgb(), Rgb::new(0, 128, 128));
assert_eq!(Hsl::new(-90.0, 2.0, -1.0), Hsl::new(270.0, 1.0, 0.0));
```

#### Hsl::new

```rust
pub fn new(h: f64, s: f64, l: f64) -> Self
```

Builds a color, normalizing the values: the hue wraps around 360 degrees, saturation and
lightness are clamped to `0.0..=1.0`, and a `NaN` counts as `0.0`.

##### Arguments

- `h` - The hue in degrees.
- `s` - The saturation, `0.0` (grey) to `1.0` (vivid).
- `l` - The lightness, `0.0` (black) to `1.0` (white).

##### Returns

The normalized color.

#### Hsl::h

```rust
pub fn h(self) -> f64
```

The hue in degrees.

##### Returns

A value in `0.0..360.0`.

#### Hsl::s

```rust
pub fn s(self) -> f64
```

The saturation.

##### Returns

A value from `0.0` to `1.0`.

#### Hsl::l

```rust
pub fn l(self) -> f64
```

The lightness.

##### Returns

A value from `0.0` to `1.0`.

#### Hsl::to_css

```rust
pub fn to_css(self) -> String
```

The CSS form `hsl(h s% l%)`, in the space-separated syntax every current browser and SVG
renderer reads: the hue in degrees, saturation and lightness as percentages, all rounded
to one decimal.

##### Returns

For instance `"hsl(210 100% 50%)"`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Hsl;

assert_eq!(Hsl::new(210.0, 1.0, 0.5).to_css(), "hsl(210 100% 50%)");
assert_eq!(Hsl::new(359.97, 0.1234, 0.5).to_css(), "hsl(0 12.3% 50%)");
```

#### Hsl::to_rgb

```rust
pub fn to_rgb(self) -> Rgb
```

The nearest 8-bit sRGB color.

##### Returns

The `Rgb` color, each channel rounded to the nearest integer.

### color::mix

```rust
pub fn mix(a: Rgb, b: Rgb, t: f64) -> Rgb
```

Blends two colors channel by channel.

`t` is how far to go from `a` to `b`: `0.0` gives `a`, `1.0` gives `b`, `0.5` the midpoint. It
is clamped to `0.0..=1.0` (a `NaN` counts as `0.0`), and each channel is rounded to the nearest
integer. The blend happens in sRGB, without gamma correction, like CSS `color-mix(in srgb)`.

#### Arguments

- `a` - The color at `t = 0`.
- `b` - The color at `t = 1`.
- `t` - How far from `a` towards `b`, `0.0..=1.0`.

#### Returns

The blended color.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{mix, Rgb};

let red = Rgb::new(255, 0, 0);
let blue = Rgb::new(0, 0, 255);
assert_eq!(mix(red, blue, 0.5), Rgb::new(128, 0, 128));
assert_eq!(mix(red, blue, 0.0), red);
```

### color::premultiply

```rust
pub fn premultiply(color: Rgba) -> Rgba
```

Multiplies the color channels by the alpha, the form a renderer composites with (a
translucent color then adds to what is underneath without a further multiplication).
Channels are rounded to 8 bits, so `unpremultiply` gives back the
original only approximately for translucent colors, and not at all for alpha `0`.

#### Arguments

- `color` - The straight color.

#### Returns

The premultiplied color, with the same alpha.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{premultiply, Rgba};

assert_eq!(premultiply(Rgba::new(200, 100, 50, 128)), Rgba::new(100, 50, 25, 128));
assert_eq!(premultiply(Rgba::new(200, 100, 50, 255)), Rgba::new(200, 100, 50, 255));
```

### color::Rgb

```rust
pub struct Rgb { /* private fields */ }
```

An sRGB color with 8 bits per channel.

Built with `Rgb::new` or parsed from text with `Rgb::parse` (`#rgb`, `#rrggbb`,
`rgb(r, g, b)` or one of the 17 basic CSS color names). `Display` writes the `#rrggbb` form.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgb;

let orange = Rgb::parse("#ff8800")?;
assert_eq!((orange.r(), orange.g(), orange.b()), (255, 136, 0));
assert_eq!(orange.to_string(), "#ff8800");
assert_eq!(Rgb::parse("rgb(0, 128, 255)")?, Rgb::new(0, 128, 255));
assert_eq!(Rgb::parse("Red")?.to_hex(), "#ff0000");
```

#### Rgb::new

```rust
pub fn new(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8) -> Self
```

Builds a color from its three channels.

##### Arguments

- `r` - Red, `0..=255`.
- `g` - Green, `0..=255`.
- `b` - Blue, `0..=255`.

##### Returns

The color.

#### Rgb::parse

```rust
pub fn parse(text: &str) -> Result<Self, ParseColorError>
```

Parses a color written as `#rgb`, `#rrggbb`, `rgb(r, g, b)` or a basic CSS color name.

Surrounding whitespace is ignored, hex digits and names are case-insensitive. `#rgb`
repeats each digit (`#f80` is `#ff8800`). In `rgb(...)` the three whole numbers (`0..=255`)
may be separated by commas or spaces. The names are the 17 basic CSS keywords: `black`,
`silver`, `gray`, `white`, `maroon`, `red`, `purple`, `fuchsia`, `green`, `lime`, `olive`,
`yellow`, `navy`, `blue`, `teal`, `aqua` and `orange`.

##### Arguments

- `text` - The color to parse.

##### Errors

A `ParseColorError` for an empty text, a `#` color with a bad length or digit, a
malformed or out-of-range `rgb(...)`, or an unknown name.

#### Rgb::r

```rust
pub fn r(self) -> u8
```

The red channel.

##### Returns

A value from `0` to `255`.

#### Rgb::g

```rust
pub fn g(self) -> u8
```

The green channel.

##### Returns

A value from `0` to `255`.

#### Rgb::b

```rust
pub fn b(self) -> u8
```

The blue channel.

##### Returns

A value from `0` to `255`.

#### Rgb::to_hex

```rust
pub fn to_hex(self) -> String
```

The `#rrggbb` form, in lower case.

##### Returns

For instance `"#ff8800"`.

#### Rgb::to_css

```rust
pub fn to_css(self) -> String
```

The CSS form `rgb(r g b)`, in the space-separated syntax every current browser and SVG
renderer reads.

##### Returns

For instance `"rgb(255 136 0)"`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgb;

assert_eq!(Rgb::new(255, 136, 0).to_css(), "rgb(255 136 0)");
```

#### Rgb::to_hsl

```rust
pub fn to_hsl(self) -> Hsl
```

The same color as hue, saturation and lightness.

##### Returns

The `Hsl` value. Converting it back with `Hsl::to_rgb` gives this color again.

#### Rgb::to_hsb

```rust
pub fn to_hsb(self) -> Hsb
```

The same color as hue, saturation and brightness (HSB, also called HSV), the model of
design tool color pickers.

##### Returns

The `Hsb` value. Converting it back with `Hsb::to_rgb` gives this color again.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{Hsb, Rgb};

assert_eq!(Rgb::new(255, 0, 0).to_hsb(), Hsb::new(0.0, 1.0, 1.0));
assert_eq!(Rgb::new(10, 10, 10).to_hsb().s(), 0.0);
```

#### Rgb::luminance

```rust
pub fn luminance(self) -> f64
```

The WCAG relative luminance: `0.0` for black, `1.0` for white.

The channels are linearized from sRGB and weighted by how bright the eye finds each
(0.2126 red, 0.7152 green, 0.0722 blue).

##### Returns

A value from `0.0` to `1.0`.

#### Rgb::lighten

```rust
pub fn lighten(self, amount: f64) -> Self
```

Moves the color towards white.

##### Arguments

- `amount` - How far to go, from `0.0` (unchanged) to `1.0` (white); out-of-range values
  are clamped.

##### Returns

The lighter color.

#### Rgb::darken

```rust
pub fn darken(self, amount: f64) -> Self
```

Moves the color towards black.

##### Arguments

- `amount` - How far to go, from `0.0` (unchanged) to `1.0` (black); out-of-range values
  are clamped.

##### Returns

The darker color.

### color::Rgba

```rust
pub struct Rgba { /* private fields */ }
```

An sRGB color with 8 bits per channel and an alpha (opacity) channel.

`Rgb` is always opaque; `Rgba` adds the alpha of `#rrggbbaa` and `rgb(r g b / a)`. The alpha
is a `u8` like the other channels: `255` is opaque, `0` fully transparent. `Display` writes
the `#rrggbb` form when opaque and `#rrggbbaa` otherwise.

#### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{Rgb, Rgba};

let glass = Rgba::parse("#ff880080")?;
assert_eq!((glass.r(), glass.g(), glass.b(), glass.a()), (255, 136, 0, 128));
assert_eq!(glass.to_css(), "rgb(255 136 0 / 0.502)");
assert_eq!(glass.to_rgb(), Rgb::new(255, 136, 0)); // drops the alpha
assert_eq!(Rgba::parse("rgb(255 136 0 / 50%)")?.a(), 128);
```

#### Rgba::new

```rust
pub fn new(r: u8, g: u8, b: u8, a: u8) -> Self
```

Builds a color from its four channels.

##### Arguments

- `r` - Red, `0..=255`.
- `g` - Green, `0..=255`.
- `b` - Blue, `0..=255`.
- `a` - Alpha, `0` (transparent) to `255` (opaque).

##### Returns

The color.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgba;

assert_eq!(Rgba::new(255, 0, 0, 255).to_hex(), "#ff0000");
```

#### Rgba::from_rgb

```rust
pub fn from_rgb(rgb: Rgb, a: u8) -> Self
```

Adds an alpha to an opaque color.

##### Arguments

- `rgb` - The color.
- `a` - Alpha, `0` (transparent) to `255` (opaque).

##### Returns

The color with that alpha.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{Rgb, Rgba};

assert_eq!(Rgba::from_rgb(Rgb::new(1, 2, 3), 4), Rgba::new(1, 2, 3, 4));
```

#### Rgba::parse

```rust
pub fn parse(text: &str) -> Result<Self, ParseColorError>
```

Parses a color written as `#rgba`, `#rrggbbaa`, `rgb(r g b / a)`, `rgb(r, g, b, a)`,
`rgba(...)`, or any form `Rgb::parse` reads (which is opaque).

The alpha of a function is a number (`0.5`) or a percentage (`50%`); like in CSS, a value
outside `0..=1` is clamped. Surrounding whitespace is ignored, and so is case.

##### Arguments

- `text` - The color to parse.

##### Returns

The color.

##### Errors

A `ParseColorError` for an empty text, a `#` color with a bad length or digit, a
malformed or out-of-range function, or an unknown name.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgba;

assert_eq!(Rgba::parse("#f808")?, Rgba::new(255, 136, 0, 136));
assert_eq!(Rgba::parse("rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5)")?, Rgba::new(0, 0, 0, 128));
assert_eq!(Rgba::parse("red")?, Rgba::new(255, 0, 0, 255));
```

#### Rgba::r

```rust
pub fn r(self) -> u8
```

The red channel.

##### Returns

A value from `0` to `255`.

#### Rgba::g

```rust
pub fn g(self) -> u8
```

The green channel.

##### Returns

A value from `0` to `255`.

#### Rgba::b

```rust
pub fn b(self) -> u8
```

The blue channel.

##### Returns

A value from `0` to `255`.

#### Rgba::a

```rust
pub fn a(self) -> u8
```

The alpha channel.

##### Returns

A value from `0` (transparent) to `255` (opaque).

#### Rgba::opacity

```rust
pub fn opacity(self) -> f64
```

The alpha as an opacity.

##### Returns

A value from `0.0` (transparent) to `1.0` (opaque).

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgba;

assert_eq!(Rgba::new(0, 0, 0, 255).opacity(), 1.0);
assert_eq!(Rgba::new(0, 0, 0, 0).opacity(), 0.0);
```

#### Rgba::from_unit

```rust
pub fn from_unit(r: f64, g: f64, b: f64, a: f64) -> Self
```

Builds a color from channels given as floats from `0.0` to `1.0`, the way Figma, Sketch
and Penpot store them. Each value is clamped to that range (a `NaN` counts as `0.0`) and
rounded to the nearest 8-bit value.

##### Arguments

- `r` - Red, `0.0` to `1.0`.
- `g` - Green, `0.0` to `1.0`.
- `b` - Blue, `0.0` to `1.0`.
- `a` - Alpha, `0.0` (transparent) to `1.0` (opaque).

##### Returns

The 8-bit color.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgba;

let orange = Rgba::from_unit(1.0, 0.5, 0.0, 0.5);
assert_eq!(orange, Rgba::new(255, 128, 0, 128));
assert_eq!(orange.to_hex(), "#ff800080");
```

#### Rgba::to_unit

```rust
pub fn to_unit(self) -> [f64; 4]
```

The channels as floats from `0.0` to `1.0`, the way Figma, Sketch and Penpot store them.

##### Returns

`[r, g, b, a]`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgba;

assert_eq!(Rgba::new(255, 51, 0, 255).to_unit(), [1.0, 0.2, 0.0, 1.0]);
```

#### Rgba::to_rgb

```rust
pub fn to_rgb(self) -> Rgb
```

The same color without its alpha.

##### Returns

The opaque `Rgb`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::{Rgb, Rgba};

assert_eq!(Rgba::new(1, 2, 3, 4).to_rgb(), Rgb::new(1, 2, 3));
```

#### Rgba::to_hex

```rust
pub fn to_hex(self) -> String
```

The `#rrggbb` form when opaque, `#rrggbbaa` otherwise, in lower case.

##### Returns

For instance `"#ff8800"` or `"#ff880080"`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgba;

assert_eq!(Rgba::new(255, 136, 0, 128).to_hex(), "#ff880080");
```

#### Rgba::to_css

```rust
pub fn to_css(self) -> String
```

The CSS form: `rgb(r g b)` when opaque, `rgb(r g b / alpha)` otherwise, with the alpha
as an opacity rounded to 3 decimals.

##### Returns

For instance `"rgb(255 136 0 / 0.502)"`.

##### Examples

```rust
use helpers4::color::Rgba;

assert_eq!(Rgba::new(255, 136, 0, 255).to_css(), "rgb(255 136 0)");
assert_eq!(Rgba::new(255, 136, 0, 0).to_css(), "rgb(255 136 0 / 0)");
```

### color::unpremultiply

```rust
pub fn unpremultiply(color: Rgba) -> Rgba
```

Divides the color channels by the alpha, the inverse of `premultiply`.
A fully transparent color (alpha `0`) holds no color, so it gives transparent black. Channels
are clamped to 255 and rounded to 8 bits.

#### Arguments

- `color` - The premultiplied color.

#### Returns

The straight color, with the same alpha.
